hooks.text: NASA was already 43 years old before its first launch.
Why did the U.S. rebrand a committee to fight a space war?
NASA didn't start in 1958; it was over 40 years old.

title: NASA's 1915 secret
description: NASA wasn't built from scratch. It was a desperate rebrand of a 43-year-old agency triggered by the Sputnik crisis.

beats.text: NASA was already 43 years old before its first launch.
beats.visual: The official National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics seal, 1915
queries: National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics logo

beats.text: In 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, triggering a wave of American panic.
The U.S. response was a disaster; the Vanguard rocket exploded on live television.
beats.visual: Vanguard TV3 rocket explosion on the launchpad, 1957

beats.text: To fix the mess, President Eisenhower signed the 1958 Space Act to create a civilian agency.
beats.visual: President Dwight Eisenhower signing the National Aeronautics and Space Act, 1958

beats.text: He rebranded the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, a research group founded in 1915.
NASA opened that October with 8,000 inherited employees and three massive laboratories.
beats.visual: T. Keith Glennan and Hugh Dryden being sworn in, 1958
queries: T. Keith Glennan NASA swearing in

beats.text: Early success relied on former Nazi scientist Wernher von Braun, who developed the V-2 rocket.
beats.visual: Portrait of Wernher von Braun at NASA, 1958
queries: Wernher von Braun Marshall Space Flight Center

beats.text: His team launched Explorer 1 in 1958, turning a 43-year-old committee into a space titan.
beats.visual: Explorer 1 satellite held by Pickering, Van Allen, and von Braun, 1958
queries: Explorer 1 Pickering Van Allen von Braun
